body: Police divers are searching rivers in Gippsland as the hunt for a missing 17-year-old enters its fifth day.

William, who also goes by Will, was last seen at about 4pm on Friday 6 November near Stoney Creek Road, close to Walhalla East, Victoria Police said. He was camping with another teenager and walked a short distance to another part of the camp to collect equipment. When he did not return, the other teen searched but found no sign of him.
He was wearing a pair of shorts and work boots, police said. ABC News reported he left his phone, food and water behind.

The search is being run from a command post at Cowwarr and has widened to a larger area of dense bush, with a police helicopter, off-road motorbikes, Search and Rescue officers and SES crews, ABC News reported. About 40 to 50 people are searching on foot.
"There's nothing that we're not doing to try to find William, and we're still very hopeful that today might be the day," Acting Inspector Jason Benbow told the ABC.

ul: If you see William, call Triple Zero (000).
If you have information, call Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000 or Sale police station on (03) 5142 2200.

body: Qantas will cut 850 corporate jobs under a deal with the global consulting firm Accenture, and most of the work will be delivered from India, the airline told staff by email on Tuesday, AAP reported.

The first phase covers finance, procurement, human resources and marketing. Some roles will stay in Australia. ABC News reported that the changes will be phased in, with the first expected from mid-2027.

Chief executive Vanessa Hudson said the overhaul was about "modernising the technology behind our business and becoming more efficient", pointing to unwieldy back-office processes and the effect of artificial intelligence. "This is hard news for some," she said, but "standing still is not an option", according to AAP.

The Australian Services Union says Qantas is using AI as a reason to move Australian jobs offshore. Angus McFarland, the union's NSW and ACT secretary, told AAP the decision "should be chilling to not just those workers but all Australians". The union says the Sydney head office will be hit hardest. Assistant national secretary Scott Cowen called for rules to protect local jobs as AI spreads, and for transition support for affected workers.

Acting Prime Minister Richard Marles told ABC News Breakfast the decision was "disappointing" and that "it's really important that Australian jobs are a focus here". He said Qantas should work with unions so that as many staff as possible are redeployed.
AAP reported that Woolworths, Coles, Canva, NAB and ANZ have also announced or flagged moving corporate or back-office work to India, the Philippines or elsewhere in Asia.
Qantas reported a 2025-26 net profit of about $1.3 billion in August, down almost 20 per cent, after high jet fuel costs, and has warned fares could rise again in 2027.

en.dek: Finance, procurement, HR and marketing staff are first in line. Qantas blames clunky systems and AI; unions call it offshoring, and the Acting Prime Minister says it is disappointing.

body: Victoria's 2026-27 skilled visa nomination program is now open for registrations of interest (ROIs) for the Skilled Nominated visa (subclass 190), the Victorian Government's Live in Melbourne website says.

The regional visa, the Skilled Work Regional (Provisional) visa (subclass 491), "is not currently open, and Registrations of Interest for subclass 491 nomination are not being accepted", according to the same website.

ul: First, lodge or update an Expression of Interest (EOI) in the Australian Government's SkillSelect system.
Then submit an ROI for Victorian nomination through the Live in Melbourne portal.
Victoria invites some people to apply for nomination. An invitation is not a visa, and you must still meet all the Home Affairs visa requirements.

body: Migration law firms that track the program say Victoria has 900 nomination places for the 190 visa in 2026-27, and that ROIs from previous program years have expired, so earlier applicants must lodge a new one. They report an ROI fee of $60 plus GST for applicants in Australia, and a nomination application fee of $180 plus GST, payable only if invited. They also say ROIs are ranked using a Victorian points test that looks at priority industries, earning potential and specialist skills.

The Department of Home Affairs has not yet published the 2026-27 state allocations on its website, which still shows last year's figures. In 2025-26, Victoria could nominate up to 2,700 people for the 190 visa and 700 for the 491.

body.note: This is general information, not migration advice. Check the official Live in Melbourne pages before you apply, and use only a registered migration agent or lawyer for advice about your situation.

उसी वेबसाइट के अनुसार, रीजनल वीज़ा यानी स्किल्ड वर्क रीजनल (प्रोविज़नल) वीज़ा (सबक्लास 491) "अभी खुला नहीं है, और सबक्लास 491 नॉमिनेशन के लिए रजिस्ट्रेशन ऑफ़ इंटरेस्ट स्वीकार नहीं किए जा रहे हैं"।

ul: पहले ऑस्ट्रेलियाई सरकार के SkillSelect सिस्टम में एक्सप्रेशन ऑफ़ इंटरेस्ट (EOI) जमा करें या उसे अपडेट करें।
फिर Live in Melbourne पोर्टल के ज़रिए विक्टोरियन नॉमिनेशन के लिए ROI जमा करें।
विक्टोरिया कुछ लोगों को नॉमिनेशन के लिए आवेदन करने का न्योता देता है। न्योता वीज़ा नहीं है, और आपको फिर भी Home Affairs की सारी वीज़ा शर्तें पूरी करनी होंगी।

body: इस प्रोग्राम पर नज़र रखने वाली माइग्रेशन लॉ फ़र्मों का कहना है कि 2026-27 में विक्टोरिया के पास 190 वीज़ा के लिए 900 नॉमिनेशन स्थान हैं, और पिछले प्रोग्राम वर्षों के ROI ख़त्म हो चुके हैं, इसलिए पहले आवेदन कर चुके लोगों को नया ROI जमा करना होगा। उनके अनुसार ऑस्ट्रेलिया में रहने वाले आवेदकों के लिए ROI फ़ीस 60 डॉलर + GST है, और नॉमिनेशन आवेदन की फ़ीस 180 डॉलर + GST है, जो सिर्फ़ न्योता मिलने पर देनी होती है। वे यह भी बताते हैं कि ROI को विक्टोरिया के एक पॉइंट्स टेस्ट से रैंक किया जाता है, जिसमें प्राथमिकता वाले उद्योग, कमाई की क्षमता और विशेष कौशल देखे जाते हैं।

Department of Home Affairs ने अभी तक अपनी वेबसाइट पर 2026-27 के राज्य आवंटन (allocations) प्रकाशित नहीं किए हैं, वहाँ अब भी पिछले साल के आँकड़े दिख रहे हैं। 2025-26 में विक्टोरिया 190 वीज़ा के लिए 2,700 और 491 के लिए 700 लोगों तक को नॉमिनेट कर सकता था।

body: ਵਿਕਟੋਰੀਆ ਸਰਕਾਰ ਦੀ Live in Melbourne ਵੈੱਬਸਾਈਟ ਮੁਤਾਬਕ, ਵਿਕਟੋਰੀਆ ਦਾ 2026-27 ਸਕਿੱਲਡ ਵੀਜ਼ਾ ਨੌਮੀਨੇਸ਼ਨ ਪ੍ਰੋਗਰਾਮ ਹੁਣ ਸਕਿੱਲਡ ਨੌਮੀਨੇਟਿਡ ਵੀਜ਼ਾ (ਸਬਕਲਾਸ 190) ਲਈ ਰਜਿਸਟ੍ਰੇਸ਼ਨ ਆਫ਼ ਇੰਟਰੈਸਟ (ROI) ਲੈਣ ਲਈ ਖੁੱਲ੍ਹਾ ਹੈ।
ਉਸੇ ਵੈੱਬਸਾਈਟ ਮੁਤਾਬਕ, ਰੀਜਨਲ ਵੀਜ਼ਾ ਯਾਨੀ ਸਕਿੱਲਡ ਵਰਕ ਰੀਜਨਲ (ਪ੍ਰੋਵਿਜ਼ਨਲ) ਵੀਜ਼ਾ (ਸਬਕਲਾਸ 491) "ਇਸ ਵੇਲੇ ਖੁੱਲ੍ਹਾ ਨਹੀਂ ਹੈ, ਅਤੇ ਸਬਕਲਾਸ 491 ਨੌਮੀਨੇਸ਼ਨ ਲਈ ਰਜਿਸਟ੍ਰੇਸ਼ਨ ਆਫ਼ ਇੰਟਰੈਸਟ ਸਵੀਕਾਰ ਨਹੀਂ ਕੀਤੇ ਜਾ ਰਹੇ"।

ul: ਪਹਿਲਾਂ ਆਸਟ੍ਰੇਲੀਆਈ ਸਰਕਾਰ ਦੇ SkillSelect ਸਿਸਟਮ ਵਿੱਚ ਐਕਸਪ੍ਰੈਸ਼ਨ ਆਫ਼ ਇੰਟਰੈਸਟ (EOI) ਜਮ੍ਹਾਂ ਕਰੋ ਜਾਂ ਅੱਪਡੇਟ ਕਰੋ।
ਫਿਰ Live in Melbourne ਪੋਰਟਲ ਰਾਹੀਂ ਵਿਕਟੋਰੀਅਨ ਨੌਮੀਨੇਸ਼ਨ ਲਈ ROI ਜਮ੍ਹਾਂ ਕਰੋ।

body: ਇਸ ਪ੍ਰੋਗਰਾਮ 'ਤੇ ਨਜ਼ਰ ਰੱਖਣ ਵਾਲੀਆਂ ਮਾਈਗ੍ਰੇਸ਼ਨ ਲਾਅ ਫ਼ਰਮਾਂ ਦਾ ਕਹਿਣਾ ਹੈ ਕਿ 2026-27 ਵਿੱਚ ਵਿਕਟੋਰੀਆ ਕੋਲ 190 ਵੀਜ਼ੇ ਲਈ 900 ਨੌਮੀਨੇਸ਼ਨ ਥਾਵਾਂ ਹਨ, ਅਤੇ ਪਿਛਲੇ ਪ੍ਰੋਗਰਾਮ ਸਾਲਾਂ ਦੇ ROI ਖ਼ਤਮ ਹੋ ਚੁੱਕੇ ਹਨ, ਇਸ ਲਈ ਪਹਿਲਾਂ ਅਪਲਾਈ ਕਰ ਚੁੱਕੇ ਲੋਕਾਂ ਨੂੰ ਨਵਾਂ ROI ਜਮ੍ਹਾਂ ਕਰਨਾ ਪਵੇਗਾ। ਉਨ੍ਹਾਂ ਮੁਤਾਬਕ ਆਸਟ੍ਰੇਲੀਆ ਵਿੱਚ ਰਹਿੰਦੇ ਬਿਨੈਕਾਰਾਂ ਲਈ ROI ਫ਼ੀਸ 60 ਡਾਲਰ + GST ਹੈ, ਅਤੇ ਨੌਮੀਨੇਸ਼ਨ ਅਰਜ਼ੀ ਦੀ ਫ਼ੀਸ 180 ਡਾਲਰ + GST ਹੈ, ਜੋ ਸਿਰਫ਼ ਸੱਦਾ ਮਿਲਣ 'ਤੇ ਹੀ ਦੇਣੀ ਪੈਂਦੀ ਹੈ। ਉਹ ਇਹ ਵੀ ਦੱਸਦੇ ਹਨ ਕਿ ROI ਨੂੰ ਵਿਕਟੋਰੀਆ ਦੇ ਇੱਕ ਪੁਆਇੰਟਸ ਟੈਸਟ ਨਾਲ ਰੈਂਕ ਕੀਤਾ ਜਾਂਦਾ ਹੈ, ਜਿਸ ਵਿੱਚ ਤਰਜੀਹੀ ਉਦਯੋਗ, ਕਮਾਈ ਦੀ ਸਮਰੱਥਾ ਅਤੇ ਖ਼ਾਸ ਹੁਨਰ ਦੇਖੇ ਜਾਂਦੇ ਹਨ।

Department of Home Affairs ਨੇ ਅਜੇ ਤੱਕ ਆਪਣੀ ਵੈੱਬਸਾਈਟ 'ਤੇ 2026-27 ਦੀਆਂ ਰਾਜ ਵੰਡਾਂ (allocations) ਜਾਰੀ ਨਹੀਂ ਕੀਤੀਆਂ, ਉੱਥੇ ਅਜੇ ਵੀ ਪਿਛਲੇ ਸਾਲ ਦੇ ਅੰਕੜੇ ਦਿਖ ਰਹੇ ਹਨ। 2025-26 ਵਿੱਚ ਵਿਕਟੋਰੀਆ 190 ਵੀਜ਼ੇ ਲਈ 2,700 ਅਤੇ 491 ਲਈ 700 ਲੋਕਾਂ ਤੱਕ ਨੂੰ ਨੌਮੀਨੇਟ ਕਰ ਸਕਦਾ ਸੀ।

body.note: ਇਹ ਆਮ ਜਾਣਕਾਰੀ ਹੈ, ਮਾਈਗ੍ਰੇਸ਼ਨ ਸਲਾਹ ਨਹੀਂ। ਅਪਲਾਈ ਕਰਨ ਤੋਂ ਪਹਿਲਾਂ Live in Melbourne ਦੇ ਸਰਕਾਰੀ ਪੰਨੇ ਦੇਖੋ, ਅਤੇ ਆਪਣੀ ਸਥਿਤੀ ਬਾਰੇ ਸਲਾਹ ਲਈ ਸਿਰਫ਼ ਰਜਿਸਟਰਡ ਮਾਈਗ੍ਰੇਸ਼ਨ ਏਜੰਟ ਜਾਂ ਵਕੀਲ ਦੀ ਮਦਦ ਲਓ।

body: Victoria's election is still more than two weeks away, but one count is already in. Ramayana: Part One was the most-watched film in Australia on its opening weekend, taking about $2.72 million from Thursday 5 November to Sunday 8 November, Variety Australia reported.

Trade publication B&T reported the film sold about 117,000 tickets over the weekend. Japan's Godzilla Minus Zero came second with $1.31 million for the weekend, according to Variety Australia ($1.6 million and about 55,000 tickets once IMAX preview screenings are included, B&T reported).
B&T reported it was the first time two foreign-language films finished first and second across a weekend at the Australian box office. The pair also held the top two spots on opening day.

"Two films in two different languages outsold every English-language release in the country," said Guy Burbidge, managing director of cinema advertising company Val Morgan Cinema. "This weekend shows how much Australia's culturally and linguistically diverse audiences are shaping cinema."

body: The Victorian Curriculum and Assessment Authority (VCAA), which runs VCE exams, confirmed its website was hacked on Wednesday, with about a week of the 2026 exam period still to go.
Around 6pm, a message from someone using the alias "DaggerElite" appeared on the VCAA home page, The Age reported. Later in the evening the site showed only a maintenance notice.
The VCAA said its site had been the "subject of vandalism" and that an initial investigation found no evidence that sensitive data or exam papers had been accessed, according to The Age.

"There is no indication that exam papers from today or previous weeks have been accessed," the authority said, according to the ABC. The VCAA said it was conducting a forensic investigation "to determine the extent of the attack". The Age reported that the authority had referred the incident to Victoria Police. VCE exams are continuing as scheduled.

The message on the home page claimed the hacker had downloaded 2026 exam papers from the VCAA's printing provider, which was not named, and sold copies to students ahead of exam day. It also claimed the papers were emailed using a law firm's address. None of these claims has been verified, and the VCAA's statement contradicts them.

GoAhead Lawyers told The Age it suspected its email address had been spoofed, that it had not authorised any emails distributing VCE papers, that it found no record of them in its systems, and that it had reported the matter to the VCAA.

The Coalition's education spokesperson, Brad Rowswell, has asked for a briefing from the Education Department and the VCAA, according to The Age and Ticker News. The Age reported that Education Minister Gabrielle Williams had been contacted for comment.
The exam period ends with language exams on 18 November, and results are due on 10 December.

The VCAA has had exam problems before. In 2024 it accidentally published material that showed questions from that year's exams, The Age and the ABC reported. In April this year the state government announced more than $222 million to rebuild the authority.

body.note: Students and parents: the VCAA says exams continue as scheduled. Check your school and the VCAA for any official update before your next exam, and do not open or share files claiming to be exam papers.

en.dek: A hacker posted claims on the exam authority's home page that VCE papers had been sold to students. The VCAA says exams will go ahead as normal and has called in police.
en.headline: VCAA website hacked mid-exams, but authority says no sign VCE papers were accessed

body: Students anywhere in Victoria would be able to study Hindi, Punjabi, Bengali or Tamil for VCE, even if their school does not teach it, under a $43 million election promise from Victorian Labor.

Premier Ben Carroll said a re-elected Labor government would expand online classes at the Victorian School of Languages (VSL) from the 17 VCE languages it teaches online now to all 44 modern VCE languages, starting in 2028. Labor also says it will explore adding Sanskrit.

"Learning a language doesn't just help young people stay connected to their past – it can unlock their future," Mr Carroll said. "Every Victorian student should have the opportunity to study the language they want, no matter where they live."
More than 16,000 Victorian students are studying a VCE language this year, and about 800 of them do it through VSL's online classes, according to the announcement.

For families in growth suburbs such as Tarneit, Truganina, Craigieburn and Cranbourne, the practical change is simple: a student whose school offers only French or Japanese could take Hindi or Punjabi online and have it count towards their VCE.

dl: Online VCE classes at the Victorian School of Languages, from 17 languages to all 44

body: Education Minister Gabrielle Williams said the investment would "give more students better access to language education". Mr Carroll added: "Labor will always back our Indian community."

In March, while he was Deputy Premier and Education Minister, Mr Carroll announced $150,000 in scholarships to train 18 Hindi and Punjabi teachers through Monash University, and $3.5 million for three schools to lead the teaching of the two languages: Alkira Secondary College in Cranbourne North and Wyndham Central College in Werribee for Hindi, and Mount Ridley P-12 College in Craigieburn for Punjabi.

Labor contrasted the promise with what it called a "$40 billion cuts agenda" from a "Liberal–One Nation Coalition". The Coalition, led by Jess Wilson, had not responded publicly to the languages pledge when it was announced on 8 November.

body.note: Election day is Saturday 28 November. Early voting opens on Wednesday 18 November.

en.dek: A re-elected Labor government would expand the Victorian School of Languages' online classes from 17 VCE languages to all 44 from 2028, and says it will explore adding Sanskrit.

body: The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) is checking retailers across several sectors for misleading sales claims in the lead-up to Black Friday on 27 November and Cyber Monday on 30 November.

It is the watchdog's third sweep of the shopping events, and the first to look at promotions in emails and on social media as well as on retailers' websites, the ACCC said on Tuesday. Australians often spend close to $7 billion over the period, SBS News reported.

body.h: What the ACCC is looking for

ul: 'Sitewide' or 'storewide' sales where many products are excluded
Time-limited offers and countdown timers that keep running after the stated end date
Pressure tactics, such as misleading testimonials or false claims that stock is about to run out
Sale prices compared against a 'was' price the product was never, or not recently, sold at

body: "Retailers risk ACCC enforcement action if they misrepresent the size, scope or duration of their sales," ACCC deputy chair Catriona Lowe said. "Retailers should not be relying on fine print disclaimers or exclusions to qualify the headline message of a promotion."

Earlier sweeps led to penalties. Michael Hill, My House and Hairhouse Warehouse Online paid penalties in June 2025 over alleged misleading sitewide claims, and digiDirect, James Lane and Vuly paid penalties in September this year, the ACCC said.

In the first nine months of 2026, 58.7 per cent of Scamwatch reports involving a financial loss were about buying and selling scams, the ACCC said. It warned shoppers to be wary of fake online shops that use big discounts and 'limited time' pressure to rush people into paying.

ul: Focus on the final price you will pay, not the promotional headline
Read the exclusions and conditions before you buy
Compare prices across retailers and against the product's past prices
Buy only if the price and timing suit you, not because a timer is counting down
Check you are dealing with a legitimate seller

body: "Consumers should be aware that a 'sale' sign doesn't always mean it's a good deal," Ms Lowe said.

body.note: To report a misleading sale, use the ACCC's consumer issue form at accc.gov.au. Report scams to Scamwatch.

en.dek: The consumer watchdog's third Black Friday sweep will, for the first time, check retailers' emails and social media as well as their websites. Here is what it is looking for, and how to shop safely.

body: A 27-year-old woman has been charged with trafficking heroin and methylamphetamine after detectives searched a unit in Mordialloc, in Melbourne's south-east, Victoria Police says.

Detectives from the Moorabbin Crime Investigation Unit executed a search warrant at the Crown Avenue unit at about 6.45am on Tuesday 10 November. Police say they found traffickable quantities of heroin and methylamphetamine, a hatchet, and items consistent with selling drugs. The release did not give the amounts.
Two women, aged 27 and 36, were arrested at the scene.

body: The 27-year-old appeared at Moorabbin Magistrates' Court on Tuesday and was remanded in custody to reappear on 4 December, police said. The 36-year-old was released and police intend to charge her on summons. Police did not name either woman.
Police say enquiries are continuing.

body.note: Anyone with information can contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000 or at crimestoppersvic.com.au. You can stay anonymous. Charges are allegations that have not been tested in court.

body: Victorians may not see a free-to-air debate between the people who want to be premier before the state election on 28 November.

The ABC invited the leaders of Labor, the Liberals, One Nation and the Greens last month to a debate broadcast on its TV, radio and digital platforms in Victoria. Labor, the Greens and One Nation accepted, but the Liberals declined, so the debate will not go ahead, the ABC reported on Thursday.

A separate debate proposed by Nine, The Age and the Australian Financial Review, between Premier Ben Carroll and Opposition Leader Jess Wilson with a rebuttal from One Nation leader Warren Pickering, will also not go ahead because the premier did not agree to the format, according to the ABC.

Ms Wilson has argued that only she or Mr Carroll can become premier, so any debate should be between the two of them. Labor argues that One Nation, polling between 20 and 25 per cent, deserves a place, the ABC reported.

A Liberal campaign spokesperson told the ABC that "engagement comes in many forms and doesn't always have to be through the media or at organised forums", and that decisions about events were made "on a case-by-case basis".

The only leaders' event the ABC describes as locked in is a town hall hosted by the Herald Sun and News24, with Mr Pickering and Ms Sandell also in the line-up. The ABC did not say whether Mr Carroll and Ms Wilson have confirmed they will take part.

In a media release on Thursday, Ms Sandell called on the other leaders to appear on the ABC. "If you want to lead Victoria, if you want people to vote for you, you should be able to get through an hour of questions without weeks of negotiations about who's allowed in the room," she said.

body.note: Early voting opens on Wednesday 18 November and election day is Saturday 28 November. Our early voting guide lists centres in Tarneit, Point Cook, Cranbourne and four other districts. The Melbourne Indian does not endorse candidates or parties.

en.dek: With 16 days until Victorians vote, the only leaders' event locked in is a Herald Sun and News24 town hall. Greens leader Ellen Sandell says the other leaders should "grow up".
en.headline: No ABC leaders' debate this election after the Liberals decline, and Nine's debate falls through too

The Melbourne Indian is an independent, free-to-read news service for Melbourne's Indian communities, published in English, Hindi and Punjabi.

Who we are

We are a small, independent Melbourne publication. We are not affiliated with any government, political party, religious organisation or community association.

What we do

We publish local news, practical guides and community information, and we translate stories into Hindi and Punjabi where that helps readers. Read our editorial standards to see how we decide what to publish.

How we are funded

We are funded by local advertising. See advertising with us.

Contact us

  • Advertising: ads@themelbourneindian.com.au
  • Facebook: facebook.com/themelbourneindian

pages.privacy:
What we collect, why we collect it, and what you can ask us to do with it.

Who we are

The Melbourne Indian is an independent news publication in Melbourne. Questions about privacy go to news@themelbourneindian.com.au.

What we collect

  • When you email us or use a form on our website with a news tip, a correction, an advertising enquiry, a directory listing or a newsletter sign-up: your name if you give it, your email address and what you send us.
  • Directory listings: the business details you ask us to publish. Once published, listing details are public.
  • Advertisers: the contact and billing details we need to run and invoice your booking.

We do not run advertising trackers on this website, and we do not sell personal information.

Visitor statistics

We count visits to the website with Umami (umami.is), a privacy-focused statistics service, so we know which stories people read and where our readers come from. It does not use cookies and does not identify you. It records the page you viewed, the website or link that sent you, your device and browser type, and your approximate location (city or region). It also counts some actions, such as signing up to the newsletter or sharing a story, without recording what you typed. We see these only as totals.

What the website keeps on your device

If you install our app or visit often, your browser keeps copies of pages and photos so they load quickly and work offline. It also remembers if you closed the "Get the app" or newsletter message, or already signed up, so we don't show it again. This stays on your device, and you can clear it in your browser settings.

Services we use

The website is hosted on GitHub Pages and loads fonts from Google Fonts, so those services receive standard technical information, such as your IP address, when you visit. Our email runs on Microsoft 365. Forms on the website are delivered to our inbox by FormSubmit (formsubmit.co), which passes on what you type and does not use it for anything else. Visitor statistics are counted by Umami, as described above. Our newsroom uses software, including AI tools, to organise and check information. We only put personal details into these tools when we need to, for example to reply to you.

Sources and tips

We will not publish your name or identify you as a source without your permission.

How long we keep it

We keep emails and records only for as long as we need them for the reason you sent them, or for as long as the law requires, for example for invoices.

Your choices

You can ask to see, correct or delete the personal information we hold about you, or to stop receiving anything we send, by emailing news@themelbourneindian.com.au. We will reply within 30 days.

If you are unhappy with how we have handled your information, please tell us first. You can also contact the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner at oaic.gov.au.

Last updated 10 November 2026.
pages.standards:
How we decide what to publish, how we check it, and how we fix mistakes.

What we cover

We cover news that matters to people of Indian heritage living in Melbourne: local and state government, business, festivals and faith, education, health services and community life. News from India appears when it affects readers here.

Sources

We report from published records, official announcements, organisers' own listings and documents we can link to. Every story ends with its sources and the date we checked them. When sources disagree, we say so or we hold the story.

How a story gets published

We sort every story into one of three levels before it goes anywhere.

Routine
Official dates, public event details, program facts and notices taken directly from an official or organiser's source. These are checked against that source before publication.
Review
Election promises, policy debates, business disputes and anything a reasonable person could contest. A person approves these before publication.
Sensitive
Crime, courts, allegations about people, public safety, health, migration or legal advice, and anything involving children. These get careful human editorial review, and legal advice where needed.

When we are unsure which level applies, we treat the story as the higher one.

AI tools

We use AI tools to help find sources, draft stories and translate them into Hindi and Punjabi. We do not use AI to invent quotes, people, interviews or images of real events. Translations are checked against the English original, and we welcome corrections from readers fluent in each language.

Politics

We do not endorse candidates or parties. In election coverage we give the same treatment to every candidate and stick to what they have said and done.

Advertising

Advertisers do not influence our reporting. Advertising and sponsored content are always clearly labelled as such.

Corrections

When we get something wrong, we fix it and add a note at the end of the story saying what changed and when. To report an error, email news@themelbourneindian.com.au.
